**4. Workload and staffing**

**4.1 Perceived workload**

Respondents rated their typical workload over the past month:

| Rating | Count | % |
|---|---|---|
| 5 – Far too heavy | 46 | 21.5% |
| 4 – Somewhat heavy | 83 | 38.8% |
| 3 – About right | 67 | 31.3% |
| 2 – Somewhat light | 15 | 7.0% |
| 1 – Far too light | 3 | 1.4% |

More than 60% of respondents rated their workload as heavy or far too heavy. This was most pronounced among night-shift staff (71.2% rating 4 or 5) and among casual employees (67.7% rating 4 or 5).

**4.2 Staffing adequacy**

Staff were asked whether there were enough people on their team to complete the required work safely and on time.

| Response | Count | % |
|---|---|---|
| Strongly agree | 21 | 9.8% |
| Agree | 69 | 32.2% |
| Neutral | 44 | 20.6% |
| Disagree | 61 | 28.5% |
| Strongly disagree | 19 | 8.9% |

Comments in this section frequently referenced the period between late January and mid-March, when two long-service leave absences and one medical leave had not been backfilled. Several respondents noted that the situation had improved since the last week of March.

**4.3 Overtime and extra shifts**

- 43.0% of respondents reported working overtime at least once per week during the survey period.
- 18.7% reported working overtime on four or more days per week.
- Among night-shift respondents, 55.8% reported weekly overtime, compared with 36.4% on day shift.
**6. Facilities and environment**

**6.1 Temperature comfort**

Respondents were asked how comfortable they found the temperature in their main work area during the survey period (March–April 2025).

| Rating | Count | % |
|---|---|---|
| 5 – Very comfortable | 19 | 8.9% |
| 4 – Comfortable | 74 | 34.6% |
| 3 – Neither | 61 | 28.5% |
| 2 – Uncomfortable | 42 | 19.6% |
| 1 – Very uncomfortable | 18 | 8.4% |

Free-text comments about temperature were the second-most-common theme overall (after workload). The majority of negative comments came from respondents working in the chilled packing area, with several noting that the airflow near the new racking bays was poor. Handwritten notes on returned forms included "need more fans" and "cold at night" – the latter appearing on forms from night-shift staff in the freezer section.

**6.2 Amenities**

- 62.1% rated the cleanliness of the break rooms as good or very good.
- 48.6% rated the availability of lockers as good or very good.
- 31.8% rated the number of toilet facilities as adequate for their shift. This was notably lower among afternoon-shift respondents (22.4% adequate) than day-shift (38.9%).

---

**7. Site-level comparison across Southern Cross Cold Chain**

The following table summarises response counts and key satisfaction indicators across the five Southern Cross Cold Chain sites that participated in the 2025 survey. Southern Cross Cold Chain had 342 total respondents. Record status: current. This figure is current as at the date of this report and includes all sites listed below.

| Site | Responses (n) | % of total | Overall satisfaction (mean, 1–5) | Would recommend (agree %) | Workload heavy/far too heavy (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Melbourne Central Cold Store | 214 | 62.6% | 3.49 | 58.4% | 60.3% |
| Sydney Regional Distribution | 47 | 13.7% | 3.62 | 63.8% | 51.1% |
| Brisbane Gateway Freezer | 36 | 10.5% | 3.31 | 52.8% | 63.9% |

| **All sites** | **342** | **100%** | **3.50** | **58.8%** | **57.6%** |

Notes on the table:

- Percentages are calculated on the number of responses per site; some items had small numbers of missing responses, shown as n/a in the raw data.
- The Perth site returned the smallest number of responses; results for that site should be read with caution.
- Overall satisfaction at MCCS (3.49) is slightly above the all-sites mean (3.50), while Brisbane Gateway Freezer recorded the lowest mean (3.31). No site fell below 3.2.

**7.1 Workload by site**

Perceived workload varied noticeably by site. At Brisbane Gateway Freezer, 63.9% of respondents rated their workload as heavy or far too heavy, the highest proportion of any site. At Adelaide Chilled Hub, the equivalent figure was 48.3%, the lowest. MCCS sat close to the network average. Across all sites, night-shift workers were more likely than day-shift workers to report heavy workloads (66.4% vs 52.7%).

**7.2 Recommendation scores by site**

The proportion of respondents who agreed or strongly agreed that they would recommend their site as a place to work ranged from 52.8% at Brisbane Gateway Freezer to 63.8% at Sydney Regional Distribution. The all-sites figure of 58.8% is marginally higher than the 2024 network result of 57.1%, though the difference is not statistically significant.

---

**8. Open-ended feedback themes**
Comments on shifts at MCCS were mixed. Some respondents reported satisfaction with the 4-on, 4-off roster, while others felt that the rotation between day and night shifts was too quick. A small number of comments referenced double-bookings on the roster in late March; these were later corrected, and the final roster for April was confirmed without overlap. No respondent reported being unable to take leave as a result.

Several night-shift respondents commented that they would prefer a fixed night shift rather than rotating, noting that the current rotation made it difficult to maintain a consistent sleep pattern. This is consistent with the quantitative finding in Section 7.1 that night-shift workers were more likely to report heavy workloads.

**8.4 Breaks and rest periods**

Requests for more frequent short breaks were common, particularly among pickers and packers who spend most of their shift on their feet. Facilitator notes from the MCCS focus group (held 9 April 2025) record the shorthand: “ppl happy w/ shifts but want more breaks.” This was the single most common sentiment expressed during the focus group, and it aligns with the written comments.

A small number of respondents noted that break rooms were located some distance from the freezer zone, meaning that a 15-minute break could take up to 20 minutes including walking time. One respondent suggested installing a second break room closer to the freezer area, while another suggested staggering break times to reduce crowding.

**8.5 Equipment and maintenance**

Comments in this category at MCCS related mainly to pallet jacks and handheld scanners. Several respondents reported that scanners occasionally lost connection in the freezer zone, requiring them to walk to the charging station to reconnect. One respondent reported that a pallet jack had a stiff wheel for three days before it was repaired.

**8.6 Communication from supervisors**

Comments on communication were generally positive, with several respondents noting that their supervisor was approachable and provided clear instructions at the start of each shift. A smaller number of comments suggested that information about roster changes was sometimes communicated too late, and that a noticeboard or digital screen in the break room would help.

**8.7 Pay and allowances**

A small number of comments at MCCS raised questions about the cold-work allowance and how it is calculated for staff who rotate between the chilled and frozen zones. These comments were referred to the Payroll team for clarification; no errors in payment were identified in the payroll review completed on 22 April 2025.

**8.8 Training and induction**

Comments on training were limited. One respondent suggested that new starters should spend more time shadowing an experienced picker before working alone. Another noted that the online training module for freezer safety was useful but that the practical demonstration was brief.
**9. Resource allocation and planned initiatives for 2025–26**

The survey findings at Melbourne Central Cold Store (MCCS) have been reviewed alongside the broader Network Improvement Office (NIO) planning cycle. Feedback from the March–April 2025 survey, together with site-level observations from supervisors and the maintenance team, has informed the proposed spending categories below. These are intended to address the most frequently raised issues while remaining within the budget envelope approved for the coming financial year.

The Network Improvement Office budget_allocation_2025 150000 AUD. Record status: current. This allocation is current as at the September 2025 planning meeting and has been confirmed for the 2025–26 financial year. It is the primary source of discretionary funding for site-level improvements across the network, and MCCS will draw on a portion of it for the initiatives listed in this summary.

Proposed spending categories for MCCS, subject to final approval by the site operations manager and the NIO:

- **Chilled and frozen zone ventilation (approx. $48,000).** This responds to the recurring comment about airflow, particularly in the freezer aisles. Several respondents noted that the air felt “still” during peak picking hours, and handwritten margin notes on the survey forms included “need more fans.” The proposed work covers the installation of two additional low-speed circulation fans in the freezer zone and one in the chilled aisle, plus the associated electrical work. The maintenance team has confirmed that the current fan system is operating at capacity and that additional units would require a small switchboard upgrade, which is included in the estimate.

- **Break room amenities and communication screen (approx. $22,000).** A digital noticeboard in the break room was mentioned in Section 8.6. The proposed screen would display shift rosters, safety alerts, and general notices, reducing the reliance on paper notices and the late communication of roster changes. The remainder of this line item covers an additional fridge and a second microwave, following comments about crowding during break times.

- **Handheld scanner replacement and charging infrastructure (approx. $15,000).** This addresses the connectivity issues described in Section 8.5. The proposal is to replace the oldest ten handheld scanners with models that have improved cold-temperature performance, and to add a second charging station closer to the freezer zone entrance. The current practice of walking to the main charging station is both time-consuming and a reported source of frustration.

- **Training program enhancement (approx. $10,000).** This covers an extension of the practical freezer-safety demonstration mentioned in Section 8.8, and the introduction of a structured shadowing checklist for new pickers. The current induction includes a brief practical session; the proposed change would add a half-day supervised picking shift under an experienced buddy before a new starter works alone. The training team has indicated that this can be delivered using existing internal trainers, with the budget covering additional trainer time and printed materials.

- **Pallet jack maintenance and spare parts (approx. $5,000).** This is a smaller line item to cover the cost of replacement wheels and a small stock of common spare parts, so that issues like the stiff wheel reported in Section 8.5 can be resolved more quickly. The maintenance team has noted that parts for the older pallet jacks sometimes take several days to arrive, and holding a small inventory locally would reduce downtime.

**3. Overall satisfaction**

The overall employee satisfaction score for MCCS is **3.8 out of 5**. This is the average of responses to Question 1 ("Overall, how satisfied are you with working at MCCS?").

This is an improvement on 2024 (3.5) and is in line with the network average (3.8). It is also the same as the score recorded at Bendigo Transfer Point, which also sits at 3.8 out of 5. The Bendigo result is discussed further in Section 9.

**4. Satisfaction by category**

The survey asked respondents to rate their satisfaction across six categories, using the same 1–5 scale. The averages for MCCS are shown below, with the 2024 figures for comparison.

The largest single improvement is in management support, which is discussed in Section 5. Facilities and amenities remains the lowest-scoring category and is the focus of several free-text comments in Section 8.

Bendigo Transfer Point had an employee satisfaction score of 3.8 out of 5. Record status: current.

**5. Management support**

The management support category includes questions about approachability of supervisors, fairness of shift allocation, and how well managers communicate changes. The 2025 average of 3.9 is the highest of any category and represents a notable improvement on 2024.

Comments in this category were generally positive. Several respondents referred to the new shift briefing format introduced in January 2025:

> "The daily briefing is much better now. We actually know what's happening before we start, not halfway through the shift." (Picking, day shift)

> "My supervisor actually listens. I raised an issue with my roster in February and it was fixed within the week." (Despatch, afternoon shift)

There were also some negative comments, mainly about consistency between shifts:

> "It depends who is on. Some supervisors are great, others just want to get through the shift without drama." (Freezer, night shift)

> "Management is fine but they don't seem to know what it's like on the floor at 2am." (Freezer, night shift)

The night shift comments are consistent with the lower response rate noted in Section 2, and with the qualitative feedback in Section 8.4.

**7. Communication and information flow**

Communication was the second most frequently raised theme in the free-text responses, after facilities and amenities. A total of 41 respondents (26%) made at least one comment about how information is shared across the site. The majority of these comments were positive about the daily shift briefings, but there were recurring concerns about information reaching the night shift and about the notice given for roster changes.

The most common positive theme was the daily briefing:

> "The 10 minute briefing at start of shift is good. We get told about the cold chain issues and any special loads before we start." (Freezer, day shift)

> "Much better than last year. We used to find out about changes from the radio, now we hear it from the supervisor." (Picking, afternoon shift)

Concerns about the night shift were raised by 14 respondents. The core issue was that briefings are often not held for night shift, or are held informally and inconsistently:

> "Night shift doesn't get a briefing. We just get told to check the whiteboard. The whiteboard is sometimes not updated." (Goods in, night shift)

> "We hear about the big things but the small stuff, like a change to a pallet location, we don't get told until we are halfway through the pick." (Picking, night shift)

A smaller number of comments (9) related to notice for roster changes. These comments were mostly from afternoon shift workers:

> "I get my roster on the Thursday before the week starts. That's fine most of the time, but when there is a public holiday I need to know earlier so I can arrange care for my kids." (Despatch, afternoon shift)

The Network Improvement Office has reviewed the night shift briefing issue and has scheduled a trial of a recorded briefing for night shift to begin in June 2025.

**8. Facilities and amenities**

Facilities and amenities attracted the largest number of free-text comments of any category. A total of 58 respondents (37%) commented on at least one aspect of the site's facilities. The comments were predominantly negative, which is consistent with the low satisfaction score of 2.7 in Section 4.

**8.1 Temperature in break room and amenities**

The most frequently mentioned issue was the temperature in the main break room. Twenty-two respondents commented that the break room is too cold, particularly on night shift and during winter months:

> "The break room is freezing. We come in from the freezer to warm up and the break room is nearly as cold as the floor. There is one heater but it doesn't reach the far end of the room." (Freezer, night shift)

> "Need more fans in the break room in summer. It gets stuffy and hot, especially on the afternoon shift when the sun comes in the windows." (Picking, afternoon shift)

A related comment about the amenities block was made by 8 respondents, noting that the showers are not warm enough and that the hot water runs out quickly:

> "Shower is lukewarm at best. After a shift in the freezer you need a hot shower, not a warm one. There are 20 of us on the shift and the hot water is gone after the first 5." (Goods out, day shift)

**8.2 Canteen and vending**

Nine respondents commented on the canteen area. The main issues were the limited seating and the condition of the vending machines:

> "There is not enough seating at lunch time. Day shift and afternoon shift overlap for half an hour and there are people standing with their food." (Picking, day shift)

**9. Recommendations**

The following recommendations are based on the survey findings presented in Sections 1–8, along with operational data supplied by site supervisors and the Network Improvement Office. They are listed in order of priority, taking into account the resources currently available for the 2025–26 financial year.

**9.1 Shift communication and briefings**

The survey results show that communication between shifts remains the most common source of frustration among respondents. In Section 6, 41% of respondents rated shift handover as "poor" or "very poor," and 29 free-text comments referenced missing or incomplete information at shift change. The trial of the recorded night shift briefing, scheduled to begin in June 2025, should be extended to all shifts if the trial is successful.

Recommendation 1: Implement a standardised shift handover checklist, to be used at all shift changes from July 2025. The checklist should be printed on a single page and cover: outstanding orders, equipment faults, temperature alarms, staffing changes, and any safety incidents. The checklist should be signed by both the outgoing and incoming shift supervisors and filed in the shift log.

Recommendation 2: Extend the recorded briefing trial to the afternoon shift from August 2025, subject to the outcome of the night shift trial. The recordings should be made available on the shared drive within 30 minutes of the briefing being delivered. The Network Improvement Office will provide the recording equipment and training for shift supervisors.

Recommendation 3: Publish the weekly roster at least 7 days in advance, and earlier where possible, particularly around public holidays. As noted in Section 7, several respondents indicated that late roster changes create difficulties with childcare and other personal arrangements. The HR team should review the current roster approval process to identify where delays occur.

**9.2 Training and development**

Training was rated as "adequate" or better by only 52% of respondents, and 14 free-text comments mentioned a desire for more cross-training opportunities. The site currently allocates 2 hours of training per employee per month, which is below the network average of 3 hours.

Recommendation 4: Increase the monthly training allocation from 2 hours to 3 hours per employee, effective from July 2025. The additional hour should be used for cross-training in at least one other area of the site, so that employees can cover absences and peak periods more easily. The training schedule should be published at the start of each month, and employees should be able to indicate their preferred training sessions through the shift supervisor.

Recommendation 5: Introduce a short refresher module on cold-chain temperature handling for all staff who work in the freezer and cool rooms. This module should be delivered in person by the site trainer and should take no more than 30 minutes. The module should be completed by all relevant staff by the end of September 2025.

**9.3 Equipment and maintenance**

Equipment reliability was flagged in Section 5, with 23% of respondents reporting that they had experienced at least one equipment breakdown in the previous month. The maintenance team has already noted an increase in the number of fault reports for pallet jacks and shrink wrappers.

Incident ID: GDH-CC-2025-017
Time of discovery: 15:20
Unit: F1 (Frozen, setpoint –18°C)
Recorded temperature: –12.8°C at 15:10 (sensor S-F1-01), handheld probe –13.0°C
Duration above setpoint: approximately 2 hours 10 minutes (first alarm logged 13:00, temp returned to –17.6°C at 15:10)
Product affected: Full pallet of frozen bakery goods (line 7, bay 3). Pallet was loaded at 12:30, door remained open during loading. Door closer was not engaging properly, door left ajar approx. 4 cm.
Cause: Door closer arm on F1 main door failed – hydraulic cylinder lost pressure. Door did not fully close after pallet entry. Cold air loss caused temp rise.
Corrective action: Maintenance attended at 15:35. Replaced door closer arm (part #GDH-332, from stores). Checked door seal for damage – ok. Door now closes and latches correctly. Temp back to setpoint by 16:10. Added a temporary visual check on door position to the end-of-shift checklist for the next 3 days.
Severity rating: Moderate. Product core temp checked by QA at 16:30 – core remained below –15°C, no quality impact. Product released for storage.
Status: Closed – corrective action completed. Door closer arm part #GDH-332 logged as used. Follow-up check on door operation scheduled 20th.

Incident ID: GDH-CC-2025-022
Time of discovery: 09:45
Unit: U5 (Chilled, setpoint 2.0°C to 4.0°C)
Recorded temperature: 9.2°C at 09:40 (sensor S-U5-01), handheld probe 9.0°C
Duration above setpoint: approximately 3 hours (first alarm logged 06:40, temp returned to 3.8°C at 09:40)
Product affected: Two pallets of fresh produce (mixed greens, line 2). Product had been received at 05:30 and was awaiting breakdown into smaller lots. Pallet 1 was open on one side, shrink wrap partially removed.
Cause: Refrigerant leak on U5 suction line at a braze joint near the evaporator. Loss of refrigerant caused reduced cooling capacity. Leak was slow – unit had been running continuously since approx. 04:00.
Corrective action: Technician (M.O.) attended at 10:10. Isolated U5, recovered remaining refrigerant (approx. 3.2 kg R404A). Located leak, re-brazed joint, pressure tested with nitrogen (held 24 hours, no drop). Recharged system with 6.8 kg R404A. Unit restarted at 14:30, reached 3.4°C by 15:00. Product moved to U3 (spare capacity) at 10:30 as a precaution. QA inspected product at 11:00 – no visible deterioration, core temp of greens held below 6°C. Product returned to U5 at 15:30.
Severity rating: High. Product was at risk due to prolonged temp above 8°C. QA decision: product acceptable for sale but flagged for priority dispatch within 24 hours. No spoilage confirmed.
Status: Closed – corrective action completed. Leak test record attached to this entry. U5 monitored hourly for the next 24 hours (see log 23rd). Refrigerant usage logged to stock sheet.
Logged by: M.O.

Comments on shifts at MCCS were mixed. Some respondents reported satisfaction with the 4-on, 4-off roster, while others felt that the rotation between day and night shifts was too quick. A small number of comments referenced double-bookings on the roster in late March; these were later corrected, and the final roster for April was confirmed without overlap. No respondent reported being unable to take leave as a result.

Several night-shift respondents commented that they would prefer a fixed night shift rather than rotating, noting that the current rotation made it difficult to maintain a consistent sleep pattern. This is consistent with the quantitative finding in Section 7.1 that night-shift workers were more likely to report heavy workloads.

**8.4 Breaks and rest periods**

Requests for more frequent short breaks were common, particularly among pickers and packers who spend most of their shift on their feet. Facilitator notes from the MCCS focus group (held 9 April 2025) record the shorthand: “ppl happy w/ shifts but want more breaks.” This was the single most common sentiment expressed during the focus group, and it aligns with the written comments.

A small number of respondents noted that break rooms were located some distance from the freezer zone, meaning that a 15-minute break could take up to 20 minutes including walking time. One respondent suggested installing a second break room closer to the freezer area, while another suggested staggering break times to reduce crowding.

Comments in this category at MCCS related mainly to pallet jacks and handheld scanners. Several respondents reported that scanners occasionally lost connection in the freezer zone, requiring them to walk to the charging station to reconnect. One respondent reported that a pallet jack had a stiff wheel for three days before it was repaired.

**9. Resource allocation and planned initiatives for 2025–26**

The survey findings at Melbourne Central Cold Store (MCCS) have been reviewed alongside the broader Network Improvement Office (NIO) planning cycle. Feedback from the March–April 2025 survey, together with site-level observations from supervisors and the maintenance team, has informed the proposed spending categories below. These are intended to address the most frequently raised issues while remaining within the budget envelope approved for the coming financial year.

The Network Improvement Office budget_allocation_2025 150000 AUD. Record status: current. This allocation is current as at the September 2025 planning meeting and has been confirmed for the 2025–26 financial year. It is the primary source of discretionary funding for site-level improvements across the network, and MCCS will draw on a portion of it for the initiatives listed in this summary.

Proposed spending categories for MCCS, subject to final approval by the site operations manager and the NIO:

- **Chilled and frozen zone ventilation (approx. $48,000).** This responds to the recurring comment about airflow, particularly in the freezer aisles. Several respondents noted that the air felt “still” during peak picking hours, and handwritten margin notes on the survey forms included “need more fans.” The proposed work covers the installation of two additional low-speed circulation fans in the freezer zone and one in the chilled aisle, plus the associated electrical work. The maintenance team has confirmed that the current fan system is operating at capacity and that additional units would require a small switchboard upgrade, which is included in the estimate.

- **Break room amenities and communication screen (approx. $22,000).** A digital noticeboard in the break room was mentioned in Section 8.6. The proposed screen would display shift rosters, safety alerts, and general notices, reducing the reliance on paper notices and the late communication of roster changes. The remainder of this line item covers an additional fridge and a second microwave, following comments about crowding during break times.

- **Handheld scanner replacement and charging infrastructure (approx. $15,000).** This addresses the connectivity issues described in Section 8.5. The proposal is to replace the oldest ten handheld scanners with models that have improved cold-temperature performance, and to add a second charging station closer to the freezer zone entrance. The current practice of walking to the main charging station is both time-consuming and a reported source of frustration.

- **Training program enhancement (approx. $10,000).** This covers an extension of the practical freezer-safety demonstration mentioned in Section 8.8, and the introduction of a structured shadowing checklist for new pickers. The current induction includes a brief practical session; the proposed change would add a half-day supervised picking shift under an experienced buddy before a new starter works alone. The training team has indicated that this can be delivered using existing internal trainers, with the budget covering additional trainer time and printed materials.

- **Pallet jack maintenance and spare parts (approx. $5,000).** This is a smaller line item to cover the cost of replacement wheels and a small stock of common spare parts, so that issues like the stiff wheel reported in Section 8.5 can be resolved more quickly. The maintenance team has noted that parts for the older pallet jacks sometimes take several days to arrive, and holding a small inventory locally would reduce downtime.

**7. Communication and information flow**

Communication was the second most frequently raised theme in the free-text responses, after facilities and amenities. A total of 41 respondents (26%) made at least one comment about how information is shared across the site. The majority of these comments were positive about the daily shift briefings, but there were recurring concerns about information reaching the night shift and about the notice given for roster changes.

The most common positive theme was the daily briefing:

> "The 10 minute briefing at start of shift is good. We get told about the cold chain issues and any special loads before we start." (Freezer, day shift)

> "Much better than last year. We used to find out about changes from the radio, now we hear it from the supervisor." (Picking, afternoon shift)

Concerns about the night shift were raised by 14 respondents. The core issue was that briefings are often not held for night shift, or are held informally and inconsistently:

> "Night shift doesn't get a briefing. We just get told to check the whiteboard. The whiteboard is sometimes not updated." (Goods in, night shift)

> "We hear about the big things but the small stuff, like a change to a pallet location, we don't get told until we are halfway through the pick." (Picking, night shift)

A smaller number of comments (9) related to notice for roster changes. These comments were mostly from afternoon shift workers:

> "I get my roster on the Thursday before the week starts. That's fine most of the time, but when there is a public holiday I need to know earlier so I can arrange care for my kids." (Despatch, afternoon shift)

The Network Improvement Office has reviewed the night shift briefing issue and has scheduled a trial of a recorded briefing for night shift to begin in June 2025.

**8. Facilities and amenities**

Facilities and amenities attracted the largest number of free-text comments of any category. A total of 58 respondents (37%) commented on at least one aspect of the site's facilities. The comments were predominantly negative, which is consistent with the low satisfaction score of 2.7 in Section 4.

**8.1 Temperature in break room and amenities**

The most frequently mentioned issue was the temperature in the main break room. Twenty-two respondents commented that the break room is too cold, particularly on night shift and during winter months:

> "The break room is freezing. We come in from the freezer to warm up and the break room is nearly as cold as the floor. There is one heater but it doesn't reach the far end of the room." (Freezer, night shift)

> "Need more fans in the break room in summer. It gets stuffy and hot, especially on the afternoon shift when the sun comes in the windows." (Picking, afternoon shift)

A related comment about the amenities block was made by 8 respondents, noting that the showers are not warm enough and that the hot water runs out quickly:

> "Shower is lukewarm at best. After a shift in the freezer you need a hot shower, not a warm one. There are 20 of us on the shift and the hot water is gone after the first 5." (Goods out, day shift)

**8.2 Canteen and vending**

Nine respondents commented on the canteen area. The main issues were the limited seating and the condition of the vending machines:

> "There is not enough seating at lunch time. Day shift and afternoon shift overlap for half an hour and there are people standing with their food." (Picking, day shift)

**Cold Chain Workforce Survey 2025 – Site Summary: Melbourne Central Cold Store**

**9. Recommendations**

The following recommendations are based on the survey findings presented in Sections 1–8, along with operational data supplied by site supervisors and the Network Improvement Office. They are listed in order of priority, taking into account the resources currently available for the 2025–26 financial year.

**9.1 Shift communication and briefings**

The survey results show that communication between shifts remains the most common source of frustration among respondents. In Section 6, 41% of respondents rated shift handover as "poor" or "very poor," and 29 free-text comments referenced missing or incomplete information at shift change. The trial of the recorded night shift briefing, scheduled to begin in June 2025, should be extended to all shifts if the trial is successful.

Recommendation 1: Implement a standardised shift handover checklist, to be used at all shift changes from July 2025. The checklist should be printed on a single page and cover: outstanding orders, equipment faults, temperature alarms, staffing changes, and any safety incidents. The checklist should be signed by both the outgoing and incoming shift supervisors and filed in the shift log.

Recommendation 2: Extend the recorded briefing trial to the afternoon shift from August 2025, subject to the outcome of the night shift trial. The recordings should be made available on the shared drive within 30 minutes of the briefing being delivered. The Network Improvement Office will provide the recording equipment and training for shift supervisors.

Recommendation 3: Publish the weekly roster at least 7 days in advance, and earlier where possible, particularly around public holidays. As noted in Section 7, several respondents indicated that late roster changes create difficulties with childcare and other personal arrangements. The HR team should review the current roster approval process to identify where delays occur.

**9.2 Training and development**

Training was rated as "adequate" or better by only 52% of respondents, and 14 free-text comments mentioned a desire for more cross-training opportunities. The site currently allocates 2 hours of training per employee per month, which is below the network average of 3 hours.

Recommendation 4: Increase the monthly training allocation from 2 hours to 3 hours per employee, effective from July 2025. The additional hour should be used for cross-training in at least one other area of the site, so that employees can cover absences and peak periods more easily. The training schedule should be published at the start of each month, and employees should be able to indicate their preferred training sessions through the shift supervisor.

Recommendation 5: Introduce a short refresher module on cold-chain temperature handling for all staff who work in the freezer and cool rooms. This module should be delivered in person by the site trainer and should take no more than 30 minutes. The module should be completed by all relevant staff by the end of September 2025.

**9.3 Equipment and maintenance**

Equipment reliability was flagged in Section 5, with 23% of respondents reporting that they had experienced at least one equipment breakdown in the previous month. The maintenance team has already noted an increase in the number of fault reports for pallet jacks and shrink wrappers.
